subject: environmental-science

moments.title: Bell Labs silicon solar cell
moments.who: Daryl Chapin, Calvin Fuller and Gerald Pearson, Bell Labs
moments.body: Bell Labs announces the first practical silicon photovoltaic cell on 25 April 1954 — 6% efficient. The first applications are powering remote telephone equipment. Early space applications (Vanguard 1 satellite, 1958) prove the technology in orbit. Costs remain prohibitively high for terrestrial use for decades.
moments.takeaway: Solar power was a laboratory novelty for 50 years, a space technology for 30, and a mainstream energy source for less than 20.

moments.title: First commercial wind farms
moments.body: The first major wind farms appear in California's Altamont Pass and Tehachapi (1980s) under tax-credit incentives. Denmark systematically supports cooperative ownership. By 2000 wind power is cost-competitive in good sites; by 2020 it's the cheapest electricity in most markets.
moments.takeaway: Persistent policy support and learning curves drove wind costs down by ~90% from the 1980s to today.

moments.title: UK legislates net-zero by 2050
moments.body: On 27 June 2019 the UK becomes the first G7 nation to legislate net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. By the early 2020s, most major economies have similar targets. The Climate Change Committee (Lord Deben/John Gummer) advises on the trajectory; the UK met its first three carbon budgets but is off-track for the fourth and fifth.
moments.takeaway: Net-zero pledges became legally binding mainstream policy in less than a decade after Paris.

now.title: Energy transition today
now.body: Solar PV is now the cheapest electricity ever recorded (~$0.02/kWh in best locations). 80% of new electricity capacity added globally in 2023 was renewable. Coal use is still rising globally (India, China) but peaking; EU coal use has fallen 75% since 1990. Batteries, electric vehicles, heat pumps and electrolysers complete the system.
now.open_questions: Can grid infrastructure, storage and permitting keep up with renewable deployment? Industrial decarbonisation and aviation remain hard.

reflection: The IEA spent two decades systematically under-projecting solar deployment, then over-corrected. Energy forecasts get the speed of change wrong in both directions; structural shifts are hard to predict.
